title: Koko Eating Bananas
corePattern: Binary Search on Answer (Monotonic Search Space)
interviewTips: Ask to confirm Koko can eat at most one pile per hour split across hours but cannot mix piles in same hour, so cost is sum of ceil(pile / k).
Point out monotonicity: if speed k works, any speed > k also works, which enables binary search vs linear scan trade-off.
Clarify constraints: n <= h <= 1e9 and pile size up to 1e9, so use 64-bit for hours sum and ceil division (p + k - 1) / k to avoid float and overflow.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Linear Search
approaches.intuition: Try eating speeds k = 1,2,3,... in order and return the first speed that finishes within h hours. Larger k can only reduce hours, so the first feasible k is minimal.
approaches.theory: Define hours(k) = sum ceil(piles[i] / k). hours(k) is non-increasing in k. Brute force evaluates hours(k) for k starting at 1 and increments until hours(k) <= h. Correct because we check speeds in increasing order. Uses integer ceil as (p + k - 1) // k.

timeComplexity.explanation: M = max(piles). In worst case we try up to M speeds and each check scans n piles. For M up to 1e9 this TLEs, used only as baseline.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only counters for speed and hours, no extra storage proportional to input.

edgeCases: Single pile [1000000000] with h=1 requires k=max pile, linear scan is extremely slow
h == n (must finish each pile in 1 hour) answer is max(piles)
h very large: answer is 1, brute force returns immediately
Use integer ceil to avoid floating point precision errors

approaches.name: Approach 2: Optimal Binary Search on Answer
approaches.intuition: Feasibility is monotonic: if k works, k+1 works. So the feasible speeds form a sorted boolean array [false,...,false,true,...,true]. Binary search for first true instead of scanning linearly.
approaches.theory: Search space is k in [1, max(piles)]. Upper bound max(piles) always works because each pile takes 1 hour and n <= h. Maintain invariant: answer in [lo, hi]. Let mid = (lo+hi)/2. If hours(mid) <= h, answer <= mid so hi=mid else answer > mid so lo=mid+1. Loop until lo==hi. This is classic lower-bound binary search on monotonic predicate.

timeComplexity.explanation: M = max(piles). Binary search needs O(log M) iterations (at most 30) and each iteration sums over n piles with O(1) ceil division.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only lo, hi, mid and hours accumulator, constant extra space.

steps: lo=1, hi=11, mid=6: hours=1+1+2+2=6 <=8 feasible => hi=6
lo=1, hi=6, mid=3: hours=1+2+3+4=10 >8 not feasible => lo=4
lo=4, hi=6, mid=5: hours=1+2+2+3=8 <=8 feasible => hi=5
lo=4, hi=5, mid=4: hours=1+2+2+3=8 <=8 feasible => hi=4

edgeCases: n=1, piles=[x], h=1 => lo=1 hi=x, binary search converges to x
h == piles.length => answer must be max(piles), predicate only true at hi
Large values up to 1e9: use long for hours sum and lo+(hi-lo)/2 to avoid overflow
Early exit optimization: break sum loop if hours already > h to save time
